inflammatory

in-FLAM-uh-tor-ee — contains 'flame'; inflammatory words are meant to set tempers on fire. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Inflammatory is intended or likely to provoke anger, outrage, or violence.

The senator's inflammatory speech was blamed for turning a calm debate into a shouting match.

Example

A commentator posts an article calling an entire group of people lazy and dishonest, with no evidence to back it up. Within hours, furious comments flood in and the post is shared thousands of times.

Language deliberately designed to make people furious is inflammatory. Unlike 'blunt,' which just means direct, inflammatory language is meant to provoke outrage rather than simply state a fact plainly.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

provocative: Provocative means intended to provoke a strong reaction — but the reaction can be thought, debate, or shock as easily as rage, and a provocative essay can be admired. Inflammatory is narrower and always hostile: inflammatory words aim at anger, outrage, or even violence, never mere lively discussion.

incendiary: Incendiary literally means fire-starting, and applied to words it is inflammatory's closest twin: both ignite anger. Incendiary runs slightly hotter — it suggests the speaker is deliberately throwing a match into dry tinder, courting real conflict, while inflammatory covers anything likely to provoke outrage, deliberate or not.

volatile: Volatile describes a person, mood, or situation liable to erupt suddenly — a volatile temper, a volatile market. It points at the thing that might explode. Inflammatory points at what lights the fuse: language meant to make other people erupt.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

soothing: calming, easing tension

diplomatic: tactful and careful not to offend

Where it sits · how strongly the words stir people up — blunt → inflammatory → seditious

blunt vs. inflammatory: Blunt is weaker than inflammatory — blunt speech is simply direct and may upset people accidentally, while inflammatory speech is deliberately designed to provoke outrage.

seditious vs. inflammatory: Seditious is stronger than inflammatory: inflammatory language stirs up anger, but seditious language goes further, actively urging people to rebel against authority.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-

Prefix — in-: into (Latin)

Root — flamm

Root — flamm: flame, fire (from Latin flamma, 'flame')

Suffix — -atory

Suffix — -atory: relating to, tending to (Latin -atorius)

Put it together

Put it together: In- ('into') + flamm ('flame, fire' — from Latin flamma) + -atory ('relating to, tending to'): inflammatory literally describes something that sets emotions on fire — words meant to spark burning anger.

Use the root in a new word: flammable

Use the root in a new word: flammable: The warning label reminded everyone that the cleaning solvent was highly flammable.
